analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on August 5, 2025 and sent to three House committees — House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary — where no action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal ethics law to make it illegal for members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children to buy or sell stocks, commodities, or futures while serving. Members would have to sell existing individual holdings or place them in a qualified blind trust — a fund run by an outside trustee who cannot tell the member what it holds. The bill also tightens enforcement: members who fail to comply face a fine equal to a month's pay (or 10% of the un-divested asset's value) for every 30 days of delay, missed transaction reports under the STOCK Act would draw a $500 fine, and financial disclosures would have to be posted online in searchable form. Exemptions cover diversified mutual funds and ETFs, Treasury bonds, municipal bonds, and assets tied to a spouse's own job or board service.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the public gains a rule that members cannot personally buy or sell individual stocks, commodities, or futures while in office — closing the gap where lawmakers vote on bills affecting companies they or their spouses hold. Members' families would have to divest or place holdings in approved blind trusts within months, and disclosure records would become searchable online. Members who simply follow the rules keep diversified index funds and their salary, so compliance is achievable; the public benefit is not having lawmakers' personal portfolios tied to industries they regulate.

how_it_helps.text: It bars Members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children from buying or selling stocks, commodities, futures, and similar investments while in office [S2].

It requires existing covered holdings to be divested or placed in an approved qualified blind trust, with the trustee — a financial institution — required to sell the original holdings so the member no longer controls them [S2].
It imposes escalating civil penalties: a fine equal to the greater of a month's salary or 10% of the value of a noncompliant holding, assessed every 30 days until the member complies [S2].
It requires financial disclosure filings to be published online in searchable, downloadable form, and adds a $500 fine for each missed transaction report under the STOCK Act [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families bear the cost: they would have to divest individual stocks within about four to six months or hand them to blind trusts, give up active control of those assets while in office, and pay escalating monthly fines for noncompliance. Spouses who trade professionally get carve-outs, but the constraint on members is real.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The ban exempts a spouse's work-related securities, board-service compensation, small-business stakes, and holdings valued under $10,000 for dependent children, so family financial interests can persist at the edges of the ban [S2].

Members must divest or lock existing holdings into blind trusts within roughly 120–270 days of the effective date, and face civil penalties equal to a month's pay or 10% of the value of noncompliant holdings for every 30 days of delay — a real constraint on how members manage their own finances [S2].

Critics of stock-trading bans argue that ethics rules and disclosure already address insider trading and that the ban would push officials' wealth into less transparent vehicles; this objection is general and not tied to this bill's text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — removing an obvious conflict of interest where the people who write laws can personally profit from them — is real and the bill is reasonably designed: it allows diversified funds and spousal work assets, forces existing holdings to be sold or put in genuinely blind trusts, and attaches escalating penalties. The costs are modest: members lose flexibility in managing their own savings, blind-trust administration is burdensome, and the spouse and dependent carve-outs create edges a determined lawmaker could exploit. The chief objection is that no such ban stops the underlying problem of insider access; but that is an argument for disclosure enforcement, not against the ban.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on August 5, 2025 and referred to the House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary committees, where it has sat with no hearings, no markups, and no floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: The only recorded action since introduction is the referral to three committees on August 5, 2025; no committee has taken the bill up since [S4].
The bill remains pending in the 119th Congress, which runs through January 3, 2027 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened yet, no one has gained or lost. If it stalls, the beneficiaries will be current members who keep the ability to trade stocks while in office.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; if it stalls, sitting members

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan but thinly supported so far: 10 of 217 House Democrats and 6 of 223 House Republicans have cosponsored, and no committee vote or floor vote has occurred to reveal a partisan split.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their households
industries.note: Members and their families would have to divest individual stocks or place them in approved blind trusts and could no longer trade them, with escalating monthly fines for noncompliance. The bill's entire purpose is to remove this group's ability to trade on legislative knowledge.

The bill channels members' assets through qualified blind trusts whose trustees must be financial institutions, creating a mandated service market while imposing strict duties and penalties on trustees. It is a niche but direct effect.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat untouched in three committees since August 2025. Bills referred to multiple committees rarely advance, and congressional stock-trading bans have repeatedly stalled despite broad public support, because they directly restrict sitting members' own finances. Without a committee markup or a discharge petition, the most likely path is that it dies at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote; reintroduction in a future Congress would be the usual next step.
